title: Ski Jumping: overview
d: Ski Jumping is a winter aerial sport played individual.
definition: Ski Jumping is a winter aerial sport played individual.
description: Ski Jumping is a winter aerial sport. highest distance + style points total wins. The contest is played individual, and the side that distance points plus 3 style scores; highest total across jumps wins. Modern jumping from 19th-century Norway; Olympic since 1924. The sport is governed by official laws that cover the field of play, equipment, players, officials, scoring, fouls, and conduct; this database walks through every one of those areas so a newcomer can follow a full match with understanding.

title: The objective
d: The objective of Ski Jumping is: highest distance + style points total wins.
definition: The objective of Ski Jumping is: highest distance + style points total wins.
description: Every rule in Ski Jumping exists to serve one objective: highest distance + style points total wins. All tactics, positions, and scoring flow from that single aim. Beginners should fix the objective in mind first, because every foul, stoppage, and strategy in the sport is judged against whether it fairly advances or unfairly blocks that objective. Coaches return to it constantly: if a play does not serve the objective, it is the wrong play.

facts.objective: highest distance + style points total wins

title: Scoring system

definition: In Ski Jumping, scoring works as follows: distance points plus 3 style scores; highest total across jumps.
description: Scoring in Ski Jumping: distance points plus 3 style scores; highest total across jumps. Knowing exactly what counts, and how much, changes how you watch: every attack is shaped by the scoring system, and comebacks are measured against it. Scorekeepers record each score the moment it happens, and at most levels the scoreboard is the official record unless a protest is filed under the competition rules.

title: How games are won
d: Ski Jumping: distance points plus 3 style scores; highest total across jumps.
definition: Ski Jumping: distance points plus 3 style scores; highest total across jumps.
description: Winning Ski Jumping comes down to the scoreboard: distance points plus 3 style scores; highest total across jumps. Because of that, late-game strategy everywhere in the sport is clock-and-score management — protecting a lead or chasing one changes every decision, from how much risk to take to when to slow play down or speed it up. Champions are often simply the teams that manage the winning condition best in the final minutes.

title: Ties and tiebreakers
d: Tied games in Ski Jumping are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
definition: Tied games in Ski Jumping are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
description: Not every contest in Ski Jumping can end tied: league games may allow draws while knockout games must produce a winner through extra time, tiebreak procedures, or shootouts defined by the competition. Tiebreak rules are announced before play and never invented mid-game; players and coaches must know them, because they reshape tactics — a team may play for penalties, or gamble everything to avoid them.

title: Match duration
d: Ski Jumping contests last: jumps last ~5 seconds of flight.
definition: Ski Jumping contests last: jumps last ~5 seconds of flight.
description: A Ski Jumping contest runs jumps last ~5 seconds of flight. Duration shapes fitness demands: athletes train to be sharp in the final stretch, not just the first. Timekeeping is an official duty — the clock, not the players, decides when it ends, and added or extra time exists to compensate for stoppages so the advertised duration is genuinely played.

title: Periods and breaks
d: Play in Ski Jumping is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
definition: Play in Ski Jumping is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
description: The jumps last ~5 seconds of flight in Ski Jumping give coaches their main lever: adjustments, substitutions, and rest happen in the breaks. Teams plan for three phases — start fast, manage the middle, finish strong — and the side that uses its breaks better often wins the second half. Break length and number are fixed by the rules; exceeding them can draw penalties.

Gear must fit and be worn correctly — loose or missing protection can keep a player off the field, and no contest is worth a preventable injury.

title: Team size

definition: Ski Jumping is played individual.
description: Ski Jumping is played individual. Numbers decide the geometry of the game: more players means more structure and specialization, fewer means more space and versatility. Every player must know the legal team size, because playing short — or with too many — brings penalties, and planned rotations are built around the allowed numbers.

Beginners should learn one position deeply before roaming — mastery of a role teaches the whole game faster than playing everywhere badly.

title: Substitutions

definition: Substitution rules in Ski Jumping control how and when players may be replaced.
description: Substitutions in Ski Jumping are a tactical weapon governed by strict procedure: only at stoppages, only through the official, only within the allowed number. Coaches plan substitution windows the way generals plan reserves — fresh legs at the right moment win tight games. Illegal substitution procedure can cost a team a player or a penalty.

Knowing what each official watches helps players stay legal — most fouls are committed in full view of exactly the official assigned to that zone.

title: The referee's role
d: The referee in Ski Jumping enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
definition: The referee in Ski Jumping enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
description: The referee's job in Ski Jumping is bigger than blowing a whistle: enforcing the laws, keeping time, managing conduct, and protecting player safety — in that order. Players may ask for clarification respectfully; they may not dispute decisions. At every level, the referee's authority begins when they enter the venue and ends when they leave it.

title: Fouls
d: Illegal play in Ski Jumping draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
definition: Illegal play in Ski Jumping draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
description: A foul in Ski Jumping is illegal play as defined by the laws — not just rough play, but any act the rules forbid. Officials grade fouls by intent, danger, and advantage gained; persistent or cynical fouling draws escalating punishment. Smart players learn the exact line: physical right up to it, never across it.

title: Penalties
d: Fouls in Ski Jumping are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
definition: Fouls in Ski Jumping are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
description: Punishment in Ski Jumping fits the foul: minor infringements restart play for the other side, serious ones award direct scoring chances or remove the offender. Penalty rules are deliberately severe enough that fouling is never a good trade — the team that stays disciplined keeps eleven (or its equivalent) on the field and wins the close ones.

title: Discipline and conduct
d: Misconduct in Ski Jumping — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
definition: Misconduct in Ski Jumping — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
description: The laws of Ski Jumping punish misconduct on a ladder: warnings, cards, sin-bins, ejections, suspensions. Dissent, dangerous play, and unsporting behavior are treated as seriously as technical fouls, because the game depends on respect for officials and opponents. Captains are responsible for their team's conduct and speak to the referee for the side.

Beginners win by doing simple things reliably; advanced players win by forcing opponents into mistakes while making none themselves.

definition: Attacking in Ski Jumping means creating the scoring chances the rules reward.
description: Attacking Ski Jumping is about manufacturing the highest-percentage chances the scoring system allows. Good offense is patient until the opening appears, then ruthless: create space, move the defense, and finish. The best attacks look simple because every player knows the plan two passes ahead.

Those first written laws are the ancestor of every rule in this database — the game you watch today is their descendant.

The modern game is faster, stronger, and more tactical than any earlier era — but it is played under the same essential objective the founders wrote down.

Variations are where most people actually play — the full eleven-a-side (or equivalent) version is the tip of a much bigger pyramid.

title: Safety
d: Play Ski Jumping safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
definition: Play Ski Jumping safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
description: Safety in Ski Jumping is part of the rules, not separate from them: warm up properly, wear every required piece of gear, respect the foul laws that exist to prevent injury, and stop play for any head injury or suspected serious harm. No game, drill, or tryout is worth playing hurt — the laws protect players who protect themselves.
